extractedReferences.rawText: identify the exclusion constraint problem as one to be addressed by any scheduling approach. This constraint prohibits any two tasks that operate under an exclusion constraint being active concurrently (i.e. neither task can be permitted to preempt the other), and is used as a means of concurrency control for access to shared resources when building a static cyclic scheduling. With a fixed priority approach exclusion constraints can be achieved by guarding access with semaphores locked according to the priority ceiling protocol. However, if it can be shown that two tasks execute in exclusion then any resources shared exclusively between these tasks need not be guarded by semaphores — the tasks are guaranteed never to access the shared resource concurrently. Of more use in fixed priority systems is a different form of exclusion constraint between a pair of tasks — the precedence constraint: one of them must complete execution before the other can be permitted to commence. The above two constraints for any pair of tasks which are members of the same transaction can be met by using time offsets and the behaviour of the priority scheduling mechanism. We first address exclusion constraints. Consider figure 3. JA OA JA OA release windows Transaction JB Figure 3 shows the release window for task A and the active window for task B. The release window is the window in time in which task A can be released. The active window for task B is the time during which task B may be executing. Clearly, if these two windows do not overlap then task B can never be pre-empted by task A and therefore tasks A and B would always execute in exclusion. Now, in general task A can arrive in any one of the transaction arrivals, as depicted in figure 3 by multiple release windows for task A (although task A cannot then re-arrive until a further eA transaction arrivals later). From the figure it can thus be seen that the two windows can never overlap if: O J O O r O T A A B B B A t + ≤ ∧ + < + (25) where Tt is the period of transaction t (of which both tasks A and B are members). Another common scheduling constraint is the precedence constraint. With this constraint we say that for two tasks C and D that are members of the same transaction, task C must complete before task D is run. We have two priority situations: task C is of higher priority, or task D is of higher priority. In the first case we can use a similar argument to that used for the exclusion constraint: task D (of lower priority) will not execute if task C has been released before task D and has remaining computation. From this it can be seen that the condition for the precedence constraint to be met is (from equation 25) : O J O C C D + ≤ (26) Note that we have dropped the second part of equation 25, since it does not matter if task D is pre-empted by a subsequent invocation of task C 4. In the second case, where task D is of higher priority, we cannot use the priority mechanism to ensure precedence, and must rely on offsets. Therefore, for the precedence relation to hold, the latest finish time of task C must be before the earliest release time of task D, i.e.: O r O C C D + < (27) Hence we have derived conditions for both exclusion and precedence constraints. We can now return to our example task set to illustrate the meeting of these constraints: the following table lists the precedence and exclusion constraints placed upon tasks, including the results of applying the analysis of equations 25, 26, and 27. 4Here we choose to interpret precedence constraints to hold only between tasks that are running as part of the same transaction invocation; different semantics mihght, however, be attached to precedence. 20 constraint result task2 precedes task3 ü exclusion between task8 and task9 ü As can be seen, the constraints are met. 9. TRANSACTIONS AND STATIC CYCLIC SCHEDULING So far we have shown how transactions of tasks with time offset relationships can be analysed: the worst-case response time of any given task can be bounded, and precedence and exclusion constraints can be checked. We now discuss some of the ramifications of this analysis. Unrelated strictly periodic tasks sharing the same period can be incorporated into a single periodic transaction, with offsets between the tasks. Tasks with similar, but different, periods can be transformed into tasks sharing the same period by choosing a common period that is smaller than the original periods. Tasks with periods which are exact divisors of a given transaction period can also be incorporated into the transaction by adding multiple instances of the same task with offsets between them. The offset approach is more general than this, however, since it allows any instance to have different attributes (e.g. priority). This generality can be used to increase the schedulability (for example, if just one instance of a task were unschedulable the priority of just that instance could be increased). The above description of constructing transactions will be familiar: it is exactly the procedure that is adopted in finding static cyclic schedules. We can take this further and argue that any system that can be feasibly scheduled using a static cyclic scheduling approach can also be feasibly scheduled using fixed priority scheduling and offsets. This section applies the analysis of this report to the problem task sets discussed by Xu and Parnas

extractedReferences.rawText: (example 2). EXAMPLE 1 In this example we take the task set given by Xu and Parnas and apply the analysis of this report. The problem is an interesting one for several reasons. Firstly, it has precedence and exclusion constraints, as described earlier. Secondly, all tasks are of the same period, and can be incorporated into a single transaction — for a single transaction the tractable offset analysis is equivalent to the exact offset analysis, and thus the results are exact. Thirdly, Xu and Parnas use the example to assert that no fixed priority scheduling approach can schedule such a system, because of the ‘inserted idle time’ problem: “Static priority-driven schemes are only capable of producing a very limited subset of the possible schedules for a given set of processes. This severely restricts the capability 21 of priority-driven schemes to satisfy timing and resource sharing constraints at runtime” They go on to say: “An example is shown where it is assumed that process segment B is not allowed to preempt process segment A. The timing constraints then require that the processor must be left idle between time 0 and 11, even though A’s release time is 0; if A starts it would cause B to miss its deadline. Note that in this example, some segments are preemptable, bit others are not. In most real situations, there will be process segments that cannot be pre-empted because a critical sectio has been enetered. Thus this example illustrates a very common situation. Neither static nor ‘dynamic’ priority-driven schemes can deal properly with such situations.” The following table gives the task set and the timing requirements, using the notation of Xu and Parnas: d r C A 161 0 30 B 51 11 30 C 90 60 30 D 100 41 10 E 140 90 50 where d is the deadline of the task, relative to the start of the transaction, r is the minimum release time of the task, relative to the start of the transaction, and C is the worst-case execution time of the task. All tasks are periodic with period 161. There are three precedence and exclusion constraints on the task set: 1. Task B must finish before task D starts executing 2. Task A cannot be pre-empted by task D (and vice versa) 3. Task A cannot be pre-empted by task B (and vice versa) We can transform the above task set into a form that the tractable offset analysis can be applied to: D O C pri A 110 51 30 5 B 40 11 30 1 C 30 60 30 3 D 59 41 10 2 E 50 90 50 4 22 All the tasks are members of a single transaction of period 161. The deadline of a task is obtained from the value of d in the earlier table by subtracting the offset value. The priority ordering given can be found using the optimal priority ordering algorithm of Audsley

Figure 5 illustrates the execution of two invocations of the above transaction. task_a task_c task_d task_b task_f task_e idle 0 20 40 60 Figure 5: A STRESS diagram illustrating the execution of the example transaction 10.DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS We have derived a piece of analysis that can be feasibly evaluated for sensible task sets, and applied it to an example task set. In this section we discuss how this analysis provides the foundation for future work addressing other real-time problems. 26 One of the uses of offsets is the reduction of pessimism in the original arbitrary deadline analysis. This is achieved by ‘spreading out’ the computation of tasks so that all the tasks are not released together. This has been illustrated in the three examples given earlier. Further, the ability to schedule any task set schedulable by static means has been demonstrated Thus, if for no other reason, offsets are useful in increasing the schedulability of a given task set. However, the main motivation for offsets has been to permit the direct expression of certain timing constraints. Although this report has not directly addressed the issue of distributed systems, we firmly believe that offsets provide the means of scheduling distributed systems, member tasks of a transaction can be located on different processors, with message passing between such tasks. The use of offsets can reduce input and output jitter, which may have dramatic impact on schedulability. We have provided analysis to determine if precedence and exclusion constraints hold. Further, as has been illustrated, time offsets can be used to reduce input and output jitter. This latter reduction is very important when building distributed transactions. 11.REFERENCES
